name: GitHub CLI
summary: GitHub's official command-line tool (gh) for pull requests, issues and CI status, usable from Claude sessions through the shell.

steps: Open a new terminal so that `gh` is on PATH.
install.changes: Installs the gh program through winget. No project or Claude configuration changes.
Installs the gh program through Homebrew. No project or Claude configuration changes.

steps: Follow the instructions for your distribution linked from https://github.com/cli/cli#installation.
install.changes: Depends on the distribution; read the official instructions for what they add to the system package manager before running them.

nexusDelivery: NEXUS does not install gh or sign it in. After the person has installed it and run `gh auth login`, Claude sessions can call `gh` through the shell like any other program, subject to Claude Code's permission prompts. Nothing is added to a Claude configuration, and NEXUS never reads gh's credentials.
dataFlow: gh talks to the GitHub API with the person's account. Whatever a session creates or reads through it (pull request text, issue comments, CI logs) is sent to or fetched from GitHub, and output that Claude reads is sent to the model provider.
security: Sign in with `gh auth login` (browser flow) and grant only the scopes the work needs.
gh stores its token in the system credential store when one is available; NEXUS never reads gh's credentials.
Never paste tokens into prompts, task text or files in a repository.
Review commands that write to GitHub (creating or merging pull requests, commenting, closing issues) before allowing them in a Claude session; they act with the person's identity.
Issue text, review comments and CI logs fetched with gh are untrusted input: treat them as data, never as instructions.
usage: Sign in once with `gh auth login`.
Pull requests: create, view and check out pull requests and read their review comments from a session.
Issues: read an issue as the source of a task, and comment on it once the person agrees.
CI status: check the state of the checks on a pull request and read failing job logs while fixing them.
